text: That's the ten traps. Now, fourteen questions, one answer each. A self join? A table joined to itself, like each employee and their manager, both from employees. UNION drops duplicate rows. UNION ALL keeps every one, and it's faster. EXCEPT returns what's in the first query but not the second. Four products expected, three received. Product three is missing. CASE returns its first true branch. Six twenty is large, one twenty is medium, fifty is small. Null inside a CASE: when score equals null never matches, so Ben falls through. Write when score IS NULL, first. Coalesce returns the first value that isn't null. Null if turns a value into null, like a zero you're about to divide by. Dates: extract a part, truncate to the month, or add an interval. The names change between databases. The ideas don't. Strings: trim, upper and lower, substring, length, joining two together, and LIKE, where a percent sign matches anything. A clustered index sets the order rows are stored in, so a table gets one. A non-clustered index is a separate lookup, and you can have many. And every index speeds up reads but slows down writes, because each insert has to update it too. Roll up adds subtotals and a grand total: four regions by three categories gives seventeen rows. GROUP BY ALL groups by every column you didn't aggregate. To find duplicates, group by the column, and keep the counts over one. To delete them but keep one, number each copy with row number, and delete everything after the first. And a cross join pairs every row with every row. Two tables of a thousand make a million. Every one of these comes back when the table is a data frame. Next: pandas.
